title: Beedi workers: a century-old trade and a vanishing cover
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The Akhil Bharatiya Bidi Mazdoor Mahasangh and the question of livelihood.
body:
Beedi rolling is one of India's oldest home-based industries. Across States such as West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, lakhs of people, most of them women, sit for hours rolling tobacco in leaves at home. Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) has a federation for them, the **Akhil Bharatiya Bidi Mazdoor Mahasangh**, which appears among the 38 federations listed on the BMS website. This post looks at who these workers are, what the law gives them, why that law so often fails to reach the rolling mat, and what a fair future for the trade would look like when demand is under pressure.

## A trade built on home work

A study summarised in a safety-industry publication puts the informal beedi industry's workforce at over seven million people, about five million of them women working from home. West Bengal alone is reported to have over two million beedi rollers, and Murshidabad district about 1.7 million, roughly a quarter of the national total. Such figures come from research estimates and not from a single census, so they should be read as indications of scale. The Ministry of Labour and Employment reported in a written reply to the Lok Sabha on 17 March 2025 that about 49.82 lakh beedi workers are registered for its welfare scheme, which gives a sense of how many have at least some official recognition.

The work pattern is well known. A contractor or middleman supplies tobacco and leaves, the worker rolls beedis at home, often with help from children and elderly relatives, and the contractor collects the finished product and passes it to a larger manufacturer. The worker is paid **per thousand beedis**, not by the hour or the day. Because the work is done at home, there is no factory gate, no attendance register and no fixed shift, which is exactly why the protections written for factory workers have been hard to apply.

## What the law provides

Two Central Acts have governed the trade for nearly fifty years. The **Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act, 1966** regulates conditions of work, and its coverage reaches home workers who roll beedis from materials supplied by an employer or contractor. The **Beedi Workers Welfare Fund Act, 1976** set up a fund to finance welfare. Under that Act the fund pays for health, sanitation, water supply, education, housing, recreation and nutrition, family-welfare services and other measures prescribed by rules, through loans or subsidies and grants-in-aid to States, local bodies and approved agencies. The Act also created advisory committees at central and State level with equal representation of the Government, employers and workers, including at least one woman.

The rules framed under the Act in 1978 also required employers to keep registers and to issue **identity cards with photographs** to workers. This detail matters. The identity card is the key that unlocks welfare. Without it a worker is invisible to the welfare machinery.

The welfare fund was originally financed by a cess on beedi manufacture, but the Ministry of Labour states that the cess laws have since been repealed and the schemes are now funded through government grants. The schemes are run by the Labour Welfare Organisation through 18 regions. According to the Ministry's information:

- **Health:** 10 hospitals and 279 dispensaries serve beedi workers and their families, with mobile medical units reaching homes. Costs of serious treatment are reimbursed, with ceilings that include up to Rs 7.5 lakh for cancer, Rs 1.3 lakh for heart disease and Rs 2 lakh for kidney transplants, and tuberculosis patients can receive a monthly subsistence allowance.
- **Education:** children of beedi workers receive annual scholarships ranging from Rs 1,000 to Rs 25,000 depending on class or course, applied for through the National Scholarship Portal.
- **Housing:** eligible families receive a subsidy of Rs 1.5 lakh for a permanent house, under a scheme that has since been merged with the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana.

Beedi workers can also use broader schemes for unorganised workers, such as Ayushman Bharat, insurance and pension schemes, and the One Nation One Ration Card facility.

## The new labour codes

Both older beedi laws now fall within the new labour codes that came into effect on 21 November 2025. The conditions of employment of beedi and cigar workers are now governed by the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. According to a news agency summary, the changes include a standard day of eight hours instead of nine, with the 48-hour week retained; overtime at double the wage rate; paid annual leave after 180 days of work in a year instead of 240; a right to free annual health check-ups; and a bar on paying less than the notified minimum wage to any employee, where earlier the bar applied only to scheduled employment. Minimum wage rates are to be reviewed at least every five years, and they cover both time-rated and piece-rated work. On paper these are significant gains for a workforce that never had a medical examination provision. The question, as always, is enforcement.

## Persistent problems

Research on the trade describes a gap between the legal minimum and actual earnings. In Murshidabad, workers were reported to earn about Rs 100 to Rs 140 a day against a stated minimum of Rs 178, and home-based workers dealing with small contractors may earn as little as Rs 50 a day. Women were reported to earn about half of what men do. These are findings of particular studies and will vary by place and year, but the direction is consistent with what unions report.

Several problems recur.

- **Piece-rate pay below the minimum.** Rates per thousand beedis are often lower than the notified minimum, and the worker has little bargaining power against a contractor.
- **Rejection and deductions.** Contractors may reject part of the delivered beedis as substandard and refuse to pay for them, even though limits on deductions for rejected work exist on paper.
- **Missing identity cards.** Contractors and employers are supposed to issue cards, but many workers never receive them, which cuts them off from health, maternity, housing and insurance benefits.
- **Health risks.** Sitting for long hours in one position and handling tobacco dust are linked in studies to back and joint pain, breathing difficulty and bronchitis, and researchers have also reported links with tuberculosis, anaemia and poor birth outcomes. Workers' families often lack the nutrition to offset these risks.
- **Shrinking demand.** Health regulation and changing consumption patterns reduce demand for beedis. This is a public health goal that society supports, but it leaves rollers with no alternative work, because the same households have few other skills and little other work within reach.

## What BMS asks

The demands of the federation are practical and are connected to the facts above.

- **Identity cards and regular wage payment.** Every roller should have a card, and wages should be paid on time at not less than the notified rate, with deductions for rejection kept within the rules.
- **A just transition.** Where demand declines for reasons of public health, workers should be offered retraining, credit and alternative livelihoods near their homes, not left to absorb the loss alone.
- **Full use of the welfare fund.** Hospitals, dispensaries, scholarships and housing support must actually reach workers and their families, including the many who work through contractors.
- **Representation.** Workers' organisations should have a real place in the advisory committees the law provides for.

## What remains to be done

Three tasks stand out. The first is registration: a worker who is not on a list cannot claim anything, so the issue of identity cards should be treated as a priority and audited. The second is enforcement of the minimum wage on piece rates, which needs inspection systems that can reach homes, perhaps through the local bodies that the old rules allowed to be asked to maintain registers of beedi workers. The third is planning for transition, because a trade that is declining for good reasons still carries the livelihoods of millions of women.

## In closing

Here, as in other declining industries, the focus must be on the worker's livelihood. A policy that is right for public health must be accompanied by one that is right for the households that depend on the trade.
